note: Every number on this screen, where it comes from, and what it does not mean. The same discipline the guards in tests/ enforce mechanically.

items.label: slopes mapped
items.how: One row per documented landslide-prone slope, each carrying a rainfall series from CHIRPS daily and the routing key's default duty holder for a local road.
items.caveat: Documented slopes only. A slope nobody has recorded is not in here, and the count is not a count of all unstable ground in Nepal.

items.label: rainfall threshold
items.how: The value the above/approaching/below states are computed against, applied to every slope on every day of the 2024 monsoon.
items.caveat: A published fit for one local area, used here as a national reference. It is the single largest simplification in this map.

items.label: mapped footpaths
items.how: Every mapped footpath, track and stairway in six regions of Nepal, from OpenStreetMap, bundled for offline use.
items.caveat: OpenStreetMap coverage in Nepal is incomplete. A trail missing here is one nobody has drawn yet, not one that does not exist.

items.label: local units located
items.how: Local units that could be given a position, from the mean of the documented slopes whose titles name them.
items.caveat: 277 of Nepal's 753 local units. A position is the mean of the slopes inside a unit, not a town centre.

items.label: slopes with a susceptibility value
items.how: A national 30 m rainfall-triggered susceptibility surface, sampled at each documented slope.
items.caveat: Kincey et al. (2023), CC-BY-4.0 - the one number in this project that is not ours. It says where failure is more likely across a country, not whether a slope is moving today.

items.label: slopes with a named responsible office
items.how: How many documented slopes resolve to a local unit with an official government website, so a complaint can be addressed to somebody.
items.caveat: 119 do not resolve. Those report the office the routing key names and invent no address.
